prime.problem: Twelve financial-math cards read as twelve formulas unless you see that almost all of them answer one of two questions: what is an uncertain future payment worth today, and how fast does wealth that compounds actually grow? Without that map, discounting, σ²/2, hedging and Kelly look unrelated.
prime.fits: The map of course 10. It leans on the probability courses (cs-8 for martingales and first-step analysis, cs-9 for the normal distribution and the CLT) and splits the course into two halves: price = discounted average payoff under Q, and growth ≈ average return − σ²/2.
expect: three pricing methods for one contract
risk-neutral q is not a forecast
prime.goal: Draw the course's causal map from memory: which cards feed the pricing formula, which feed the growth formula, and which single idea (σ²/2) connects returns, GBM and Kelly.

attend: Why can a bond be priced by discounting alone, while an option needs a change of weights to Q before discounting?
The same σ²/2 shows up in the returns card, the GBM card and the Kelly card. What is compounding doing in each of those three places?
Trees, the closed form and Monte Carlo give 10.4486, 10.4506 and 10.4697 for the shared call. Which method is exact for which model, and where does each one's error come from?
In the "what the shortcut costs" chart, why do the Kelly rows have no ceiling while the variance-reduction rows are fixed ratios?
Which assumption in "When this advice doesn't apply" would break the pricing half, and which would break the growth half?

must: Money at different dates can't be added → discount each flow by e<sup>−rT</sup> (or (1+r)<sup>−t</sup>) → a certain payoff's price is just its discounted value (bonds, NPV) → an uncertain payoff needs an average first

An option's payoff can be copied with stock + cash → its price must equal the copy's cost → that cost equals the discounted average under the weights Q that make the stock earn r → trees, Black–Scholes and Monte Carlo are three ways to compute the same E<sub>Q</sub>

Wealth multiplies over time → what you end with follows the average log return → the log average sits ≈ σ²/2 below the simple average → the median path lags the mean, diversification raises growth, and 2× Kelly gives negative growth

A small edge adds n·(edge) of drift while noise grows only like √n → over few bets noise hides the edge, over many it decides everything → ruin odds, Kelly sizing and market-making edge all follow from this race
elevated: Each pricing method has its own error law: the tree's error falls like 1/N (10 → 1,000 steps: 0.1972 → 0.0020), Monte Carlo's like 1/√n → so trees win for one asset with early exercise, simulation wins for path-dependent or many-asset payoffs
reference: the shared contract's numbers (S₀ = K = 100, r = 5%, σ = 20%, T = 1 → C 10.4506, P 5.5735)
the reference list (Hull, Shreve, Glasserman, Thorp, Zhou)
the log-scale bar chart's axis choices

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the course as two trees: a price tree rooted at "discounted average payoff" with the time-value, bond, binomial, Black–Scholes, Monte Carlo and EV-games cards as leaves; and a growth tree rooted at "average return − σ²/2" with the returns, portfolio, Sharpe, Kelly, random-walk and GBM cards. Draw one arrow between the two trees and label it.
checklist: price = e<sup>−rT</sup> × average payoff; certain payoffs skip the averaging
Q comes from the hedge, not from anyone's forecast of the stock
three pricing methods compute the same E<sub>Q</sub>; they differ in which payoffs they handle and how their error shrinks
compounding means the log return is what accumulates, which costs about σ²/2 against the simple average
drift n vs noise √n decides when a small edge matters
a link between the trees: GBM feeds Black–Scholes and Monte Carlo (with μ swapped for r), or Kelly's log utility is the growth tree's version of an expected value

retrieve.q: Explain in four sentences why the price of the shared call doesn't depend on the stock's real expected return μ, even though its payoff obviously depends on where the stock goes.
answer: stock + cash can copy the option's payoff
no-arbitrage forces the option price to equal the copy's cost
the copy's cost is computed with weights under which the stock earns r, so μ never enters
μ matters for what you expect to earn by holding the option, not for its price

retrieve.q: Walk the σ²/2 through three cards: the +50%/−50% example, GBM's mean vs median at μ = 8%, σ = 20%, and the Kelly curve's zero at about 2f*.
answer: returns: average simple return 0% but the log sum is ln 0.75, a 25% loss
GBM: the mean grows at μ (108.33), the median at μ − σ²/2 (106.18)
Kelly: growth ≈ edge·f − f²/2 (variance of the bet), so doubling f makes the variance term eat the whole edge

retrieve.q: You need a price for (a) a European call, (b) an American put, (c) an Asian call on 12 monthly closes. Pick one method for each from this course and say what makes the other two worse.
answer: (a) Black–Scholes: exact, O(1); a tree only converges like 1/N, Monte Carlo leaves ±0.015 at 10⁶ paths
(b) binomial tree: backward induction can compare exercise vs hold at each node; the formula has no early exercise, and forward simulation doesn't know the value of waiting
(c) Monte Carlo: any path payoff, error 1/√n regardless of dimension; the tree would need 2¹² paths, and there is no closed form for an arithmetic average

retrieve.q: A colleague says "0.49 is basically a coin flip, and betting 0.4 of the bankroll on a 60/40 coin is just aggressive, not wrong". Which two cards refute each claim, and with what numbers?
answer: Kelly: at f = 0.4, g = −0.00245 per bet; median wealth after 1,000 bets is 0.0866, and 56% end below where they started

compare.q: The course uses "a price is a martingale after discounting" (pricing) and "r<sup>S<sub>n</sub></sup> is a martingale" (gambler's ruin). What is the martingale doing in each, and why is it the same trick?
answer: in both, a quantity whose expected future value equals its present value turns a path question into one equation
ruin: optional stopping on r<sup>S<sub>n</sub></sup> gives the hitting probability
pricing: under Q the discounted stock (and so the discounted option) is a martingale, so today's price is the expected discounted payoff
the difference is where the weights come from: the coin's real p, or the hedge's q

compare.q: Why does the CLT justify both the lognormal price model and Monte Carlo's error bar, and where does it fail each time?
answer: many small independent log returns add up to a near-normal log price, so the price is lognormal
the average of n independent payoffs has error s/√n and is near-normal, so ±1.96 SE is a 95% interval
it fails for prices when returns have fat tails or clustered volatility, and for Monte Carlo when the payoff variance is huge or infinite

predict.q: Suppose volatility doubles to 40% while everything else stays fixed. Before checking any card, predict the direction of change for: the shared call's price, the GBM median after one year at μ = 8%, and the Kelly-style growth of holding the stock. Which half of the course gets better for the holder, and which gets worse?
predict.answer: Pricing: the call gets more valuable (vega is positive; at σ = 30% it is already 14.23 against 10.45), because the option keeps the upside and caps the downside. Growth: the median falls to 100 · e0.08 − 0.08 = 100, so the typical stockholder goes nowhere, and the growth rate μ − σ²/2 drops from 6% to 0%. Volatility is worth paying for in an option and costs you in a compounding holding: the same σ²/2 on opposite sides.
